Game: This is a picture, not a game: the four free tips always make a shape whose opposite sides match.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or D to change the four-sided shape, or drag P, Q, R or S to change the triangles. Focus a point and use the arrow keys, and tick the boxes to show names, the outline or the angle marks.
Show
Look for the math

Move one point and four triangles change at once, yet their free tips still form a parallelogram. Michael de Villiers discovered this as a generalisation of the equilateral-triangle case. The page states it for any quadrilateral; the logic test tried over 4,000 random shapes, turns and scales and found no exception. The live page now shows a GeoGebra figure dated 13 March 2017; the original Java applet is visible in the 28 September 2006 snapshot of the same address.

One turn and one stretch

The applet keeps one turn q and one stretch r for all four triangles. On a side from X to Y it puts the free tip at X + r·turn(Y − X, q): start at X, turn the step to Y, then stretch it. That is a spiral similarity. Because every triangle uses the same turn and stretch, the four triangles are similar triangles: their angles at P, Q, R, S match, and so do their angles at the shared corners A, B, C, D.

Why the tips make a parallelogram

Write the turn and stretch together as one number k. Then the four tips are simply P = (1−k)A + kB, Q = (1−k)C + kB, R = (1−k)C + kD and S = (1−k)A + kD. Add opposite corners: P + R = Q + S, whatever A, B, C and D are. Equal sums of opposite corners are exactly the test for a parallelogram. This is why a crossed or dented quadrilateral works too: no convexity is needed. Tick the middle box to trace the four tips.

The ratios on the page

The page claims PB/PA = QB/QC = RD/RC = SD/SA and then that the product (PB/PA)(QC/QB)(RD/RC)(SA/SD) is 1. Both are true, and the test checks them on every generated case: each triangle contributes a ratio and its partner contributes the reciprocal, so the product is a homothety of scale 1, which is the identity. One printed detail is wrong: formulas (1) and (3) write RD/DC where line (2) writes RD/RC. As printed, that product equals the stretch r, so it is 1 only for the starting equilateral figure (r = 1); with RD/RC it is always 1. We follow the applet's construction and the page's stated parallelogram claim.

Drag P until the four triangles have a different shape, then drag A: the new shape of the triangles stays, and the outline of PQRS stays a parallelogram.
